items.stem: Which of the following best describes "noise"?
options: Creating new, more informative features from raw data using domain knowledge, such as ratios, counts or date parts
A feature-selection approach that ranks features by a statistic (e.g. correlation, chi-squared) independent of any model
Random errors or irrelevant variation in data that do not represent the underlying pattern
Detecting and correcting or removing incorrect, incomplete, inconsistent, duplicated or irrelevant data before training a model
items.answer: Random errors or irrelevant variation in data that do not represent the underlying pattern
items.markingKey: C. "noise" is random errors or irrelevant variation in data that do not represent the underlying pattern.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Min-max normalisation always produces values between 0 and 1 for new data.
Reason (R): It uses the minimum and maximum of the training data.
Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
items.answer: A is false but R is true.
items.markingKey: D. A is false – new values outside the training range map outside [0, 1]; R is true and explains why.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why outliers should not automatically be deleted.
items.answer: Some outliers are genuine and informative (fraud, rare diseases); removing them hides important cases. Only errors (impossible values, typos) should be removed or corrected. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Some outliers are genuine and informative (fraud, rare diseases); removing them hides important cases. Only errors (impossible values, typos) should be removed or corrected. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: The feature floor area (m²) takes the values 15, 56, 68, 124, 164. Using min-max normalisation to the range [0, 1], calculate the normalised value of 56.
"Data cleaning is only needed for small datasets." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Large datasets usually contain more errors, duplicates and inconsistencies; "garbage in, garbage out" applies at any scale.
items.markingKey: Large datasets usually contain more errors, duplicates and inconsistencies; "garbage in, garbage out" applies at any scale. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that Data cleaning is the most important stage of a machine-learning project.
items.answer: It is among the most important stages because no algorithm can compensate for poor data, but it must be balanced with sound modelling and evaluation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: model quality is limited by data quality; practitioners report most time is spent on preparation; errors and bias in data propagate into predictions. Arguments against: algorithm choice, features and evaluation also matter; over-cleaning can remove genuine signal; the importance depends on the data source. Supported judgement: It is among the most important stages because no algorithm can compensate for poor data, but it must be balanced with sound modelling and evaluation.

items.stem: Which is the most appropriate way to handle the category "Kenya" written as "kenya", "KENYA" and "Kenya " in a dataset?
options: Delete all three rows
Treat them as three different countries
Replace them with the mean
Standardise case and trim whitespace so they become one category
items.answer: Standardise case and trim whitespace so they become one category
items.markingKey: D. Inconsistent formatting should be standardised.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A data point that lies far from the other observations, which may be an error or a genuine extreme value"?
options: principal component analysis (PCA)
outlier
curse of dimensionality
embedded method
items.answer: outlier
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of outlier.

items.stem: Explain the difference between median imputation and mean imputation.
items.answer: Mean imputation fills gaps with the average, which is pulled by outliers; median imputation uses the middle value, which is robust to outliers.
items.markingKey: Mean imputation fills gaps with the average, which is pulled by outliers; median imputation uses the middle value, which is robust to outliers. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the statistics used for scaling must be calculated on the training set only.
items.answer: Using test data to compute means or min/max leaks information about the test set into training, giving over-optimistic evaluation results.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Using test data to compute means or min/max leaks information about the test set into training, giving over-optimistic evaluation results. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Median imputation is preferred to mean imputation for skewed data.
Reason (R): The median is not pulled by extreme values.
Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: A. Both true; R explains A.

items.stem:
A customer dataset contains these records (Name, City, Age):
Name | City | Age
Elena | Geneva | 34
Kenji | Toronto | 60
Elena | Geneva | 34
Tomas | Lima | 59
Freya | Oslo | 68
Freya | Oslo | 68
Mei | Lima | 34
Mei | Lima | 34
How many exact duplicate rows must be removed, and how many records remain? Explain why duplicates harm a model.
items.answer: 3 duplicates removed; 5 records remain. Duplicates over-weight some examples, bias the model and can leak between training and test sets.
items.markingKey: 3 duplicates (A1); 5 remain (A1); R1 bias/over-weighting/leakage.

items.stem: The following ages entered on a sign-up form are being cleaned: 60, 103, 54, 58, 55, 45, 55, 37, 7, 49, 35. Using the 1.5 × IQR rule (quartiles found as medians of the lower and upper halves, excluding the median when n is odd), identify any outliers, and discuss whether they should be removed.
items.answer: Q1 = 37, Q3 = 58, IQR = 21; fences 5.5 and 89.5; outliers: 103.
items.markingKey: Q1 = 37, Q3 = 58, IQR = 21; fences 5.5 and 89.5; outliers: 103. M1 sorted data/quartiles; A1 IQR and fences; A1 outliers. R1: remove only if errors (e.g. impossible values); genuine extreme values may carry information (e.g. real delays).

items.stem: A dataset of resting heart rate (bpm) from a fitness app has missing values (?): 80, 63, ?, 480, ?, 32, 65. Calculate the mean and the median of the known values and justify which should be used to impute the missing values.
items.answer: mean of known values = 144; median = 65. The median (65) is the better choice because the outlier 480 pulls the mean up.
items.markingKey: Known values: 80, 63, 480, 32, 65 (M1). mean of known values = 144; median = 65. The median (65) is the better choice because the outlier 480 pulls the mean up. A1 each; R1 justification (median is robust to outliers).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A feature-selection approach that evaluates subsets of features by training a model on each, e.g. forward selection or recursive feature elimination"?
options: wrapper method
outlier
curse of dimensionality
normalisation (min-max scaling)
items.answer: wrapper method
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of wrapper method.

items.stem: "More features always give a more accurate model." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Extra irrelevant or redundant features add noise and dimensionality, often causing overfitting and lower test accuracy.
items.markingKey: Extra irrelevant or redundant features add noise and dimensionality, often causing overfitting and lower test accuracy. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Filter methods consider interactions between features.
Reason (R): Filter methods evaluate each feature using a statistic independent of the model.
Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
items.answer: A is false but R is true.
items.markingKey: D. A is false; R is true and explains why.

items.stem:
A school in Kuala Lumpur wants to predict exam Score. The data are:
StudyHours | ShoeSize | PhoneHours | Score
8.3 | 3 | 21 | 83
6.8 | 7 | 31 | 71
4.2 | 8 | 45 | 49
9.1 | 9 | 17 | 88
8.7 | 4 | 21 | 81
5.1 | 9 | 52 | 42
The Pearson correlation of each feature with Score is: StudyHours 0.957, ShoeSize -0.518, PhoneHours -0.998. Using a threshold of |r| ≥ 0.5, state which features should be selected and justify.
items.answer: r(StudyHours, Score) = 0.957; r(ShoeSize, Score) = -0.518; r(PhoneHours, Score) = -0.998. Keep: StudyHours, ShoeSize, PhoneHours (|r| ≥ 0.5).
items.markingKey: r(StudyHours, Score) = 0.957; r(ShoeSize, Score) = -0.518; r(PhoneHours, Score) = -0.998. Keep: StudyHours, ShoeSize, PhoneHours (|r| ≥ 0.5). Limitation: correlation only captures linear, one-feature-at-a-time relationships; it misses interactions and non-linear effects, and correlation is not causation.

items.stem: A health model in Mumbai has raw features mass = 62 kg and height = 1.62 m. Engineer the feature BMI = mass / height² for this patient and explain why an engineered feature can improve a model.
items.answer: BMI = 62/1.62² = 23.6. It combines two raw features into one that is more directly related to the target, so simpler models can use it.
items.markingKey: 62/1.62² = 23.6 (M1 A1); R1 domain knowledge captures a relationship the model would otherwise need to learn.

items.stem:
(a) Explain why removing irrelevant features can improve a model. [2]
(b) A running app records distance = 23 km and duration = 218 min. Create the engineered feature average speed (km/h) and suggest one further feature that could help predict injury risk. [3]
(c) Give one argument for and one argument against the view that Domain experts should always be involved in feature engineering. [4]
items.answer: (a) Irrelevant features add noise that the model may fit (overfitting), increase training time and memory, and make the model harder to interpret; fewer, relevant features generalise better. (b) 23/(218/60) = 6.33 km/h. Further feature: e.g. weekly distance change, pace variability. (c) Expert involvement is highly valuable, especially for tabular data and in sensitive domains, but should be combined with data-driven selection.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] Award marks for: Irrelevant features add noise that the model may fit (overfitting), increase training time and memory, and make the model harder to interpret; fewer, relevant features generalise better. (one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.) (b) [3 marks] Convert minutes to hours (M1); 6.33 km/h (A1); sensible additional engineered feature (R1). (c) [4 marks] Arguments for: experts know which derived quantities matter (e.g. BMI, debt ratio); helps avoid nonsensical or leaking features. Arguments against: deep learning can learn features automatically from raw data; experts may carry biases or overlook unexpected patterns; cost and availability of experts. Supported judgement: Expert involvement is highly valuable, especially for tabular data and in sensitive domains, but should be combined with data-driven selection.

items.stem: Define the term "feature engineering".
items.answer: Creating new, more informative features from raw data using domain knowledge, such as ratios, counts or date parts
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: creating new, more informative features from raw data using domain knowledge, such as ratios, counts or date parts. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "feature selection"?
options: Reducing the number of features while keeping as much useful information as possible, by selection or by transformation (e.g. PCA)
A data point that lies far from the other observations, which may be an error or a genuine extreme value
Choosing the subset of available features that are most relevant to the target, discarding irrelevant or redundant ones
An unsupervised technique that transforms correlated features into a smaller set of uncorrelated principal components ordered by the variance they explain
items.answer: Choosing the subset of available features that are most relevant to the target, discarding irrelevant or redundant ones
items.markingKey: C. "feature selection" is choosing the subset of available features that are most relevant to the target, discarding irrelevant or redundant ones.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a filter method and a wrapper method.
items.answer: A filter method scores features independently of any model (fast); a wrapper method searches subsets using a model's performance (slower but accounts for interactions).
items.markingKey: A filter method scores features independently of any model (fast); a wrapper method searches subsets using a model's performance (slower but accounts for interactions). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why two highly correlated features may both not be needed.
items.answer: They carry largely the same information (redundancy), so keeping both adds little predictive power, can destabilise some models (multicollinearity in regression) and increases dimensionality.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They carry largely the same information (redundancy), so keeping both adds little predictive power, can destabilise some models (multicollinearity in regression) and increases dimensionality. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between label encoding and one-hot encoding.
items.answer: One-hot uses a binary column per category with no implied order; label encoding maps categories to integers, which implies an order and is suitable only for ordinal data.
items.markingKey: One-hot uses a binary column per category with no implied order; label encoding maps categories to integers, which implies an order and is suitable only for ordinal data. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A model uses the feature City with possible values Hanoi, Oslo, Seoul, Lisbon, Accra plus 3 numerical features. Using one-hot encoding with columns in alphabetical order (Accra, Hanoi, Lisbon, Oslo, Seoul), encode the rows Hanoi, Hanoi, Oslo, Accra, Lisbon, and state how many input features the model will have. Explain why label encoding (Lima = 1, Oslo = 2, …) could mislead a linear model.
items.answer: Hanoi → [0, 1, 0, 0, 0]; Hanoi → [0, 1, 0, 0, 0]; Oslo → [0, 0, 0, 1, 0]; Accra → [1, 0, 0, 0, 0]; Lisbon → [0, 0, 1, 0, 0]. Total features = 3 + 5 = 8. Label encoding implies an order/size between cities that does not exist.
items.markingKey: Encodings: Hanoi → [0, 1, 0, 0, 0]; Hanoi → [0, 1, 0, 0, 0]; Oslo → [0, 0, 0, 1, 0]; Accra → [1, 0, 0, 0, 0]; Lisbon → [0, 0, 1, 0, 0] (A2). Feature count 8 (A1). R1 artificial ordering.

items.stem: A model uses the feature City with possible values Accra, Oslo, Lima plus 4 numerical features. Using one-hot encoding with columns in alphabetical order (Accra, Lima, Oslo), encode the rows Lima, Oslo, Oslo, Lima, Oslo, and state how many input features the model will have. Explain why label encoding (Lima = 1, Oslo = 2, …) could mislead a linear model.
items.answer: Lima → [0, 1, 0]; Oslo → [0, 0, 1]; Oslo → [0, 0, 1]; Lima → [0, 1, 0]; Oslo → [0, 0, 1]. Total features = 4 + 3 = 7. Label encoding implies an order/size between cities that does not exist.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "dimensionality reduction"?
options: Creating new, more informative features from raw data using domain knowledge, such as ratios, counts or date parts
The number of features (input variables) used to describe each data point
Reducing the number of features while keeping as much useful information as possible, by selection or by transformation (e.g. PCA)
A feature-selection approach that ranks features by a statistic (e.g. correlation, chi-squared) independent of any model
items.answer: Reducing the number of features while keeping as much useful information as possible, by selection or by transformation (e.g. PCA)

items.stem: Alessia writes: "PCA selects the most important original features." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: PCA creates new features (principal components) that are linear combinations of all the original features.
items.markingKey: PCA creates new features (principal components) that are linear combinations of all the original features. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): The first principal component explains the largest share of the variance.
Reason (R): PCA orders components by the variance they capture.
Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

items.stem: Principal component analysis on a 4-feature dataset gives eigenvalues (variances) 7.58, 6.83, 2.96, 0.91. Calculate the percentage of variance explained by each component and the number of components needed to keep at least 95% of the variance.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that PCA should always be applied before training a model on high-dimensional data.
items.answer: PCA is a useful tool but not automatic: it should be evaluated against model performance and the need for interpretability.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: reduces dimensionality, training time and overfitting; removes correlated features; enables visualisation. Arguments against: components are hard to interpret; variance is not the same as predictive relevance – useful low-variance features can be discarded; not suitable for non-linear structure. Supported judgement: PCA is a useful tool but not automatic: it should be evaluated against model performance and the need for interpretability.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "curse of dimensionality".
items.answer: The problems that arise as the number of features grows: data become sparse, distances lose meaning and the amount of data needed grows exponentially
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the problems that arise as the number of features grows: data become sparse, distances lose meaning and the amount of data needed grows exponentially. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why k-nearest neighbours performs poorly in very high-dimensional spaces.
items.answer: As dimensions increase, the distances between all points become similar, so the "nearest" neighbours are hardly nearer than others and data become sparse; many irrelevant dimensions also add noise to the distance.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: As dimensions increase, the distances between all points become similar, so the "nearest" neighbours are hardly nearer than others and data become sparse; many irrelevant dimensions also add noise to the distance. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between feature selection and feature extraction (e.g. PCA).
items.answer: Feature selection keeps a subset of the original features (still interpretable); feature extraction creates new combined features, which may be harder to interpret.
items.markingKey: Feature selection keeps a subset of the original features (still interpretable); feature extraction creates new combined features, which may be harder to interpret. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that PCA selects the most important original features. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: PCA creates new features (principal components) that are linear combinations of all the original features.

items.stem: Each feature is divided into 10 intervals, so the feature space is split into cells. Compare the number of cells for 2 feature(s) and 3 features, and the number of training samples needed for about 5 samples per cell. Explain what this shows about the curse of dimensionality.
items.answer: 10^2 = 100 cells vs 10^3 = 1000 cells; for 5 samples per cell you need 500 vs 5000 samples. The data needed grows exponentially with dimensions, so data becomes sparse.
items.markingKey: 10^2 = 100 cells vs 10^3 = 1000 cells; for 5 samples per cell you need 500 vs 5000 samples. A1 each count; R1 exponential growth → sparsity, distances become less meaningful, more data or fewer dimensions needed.

items.answer: Explained variance: PC1 36.8%, PC2 29.3%, PC3 17.1%, PC4 11.7%, PC5 5.1%; cumulative reaches 100.0% after 5 components, so keep 5.
items.markingKey: Total variance 22.7 (M1); each % = eigenvalue/total (A1); cumulative sums (M1); 5 components (A1).

items.stem:
Case study context: Saigon Fresh, a supermarket chain in Hanoi, analyses loyalty-card transactions with association rules, forecasts stock with regression and runs an inventory system based on linked lists and stacks.
(a) A student claims that Dimensionality reduction never loses information. Identify the error in this claim and correct it. Refer to Saigon Fresh in your answer. [2]
(b) Evaluate the claim that PCA should always be applied before training a model on high-dimensional data. Refer to Saigon Fresh in your answer. [4]
items.answer: (a) Discarding low-variance components loses some information; the aim is to lose as little useful information as possible. (b) PCA is a useful tool but not automatic: it should be evaluated against model performance and the need for interpretability.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] Discarding low-variance components loses some information; the aim is to lose as little useful information as possible. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation. (b) [4 marks] Arguments for: reduces dimensionality, training time and overfitting; removes correlated features; enables visualisation. Arguments against: components are hard to interpret; variance is not the same as predictive relevance – useful low-variance features can be discarded; not suitable for non-linear structure. Supported judgement: PCA is a useful tool but not automatic: it should be evaluated against model performance and the need for interpretability. Case study context: Sabana Health, a network of clinics in Bogotá, is moving patient records into a relational database and trialling a machine-learning triage tool; its booking app is written in an object-oriented language.
(a) With the help of a specific example, explain why k-nearest neighbours performs poorly in very high-dimensional spaces. Refer to Sabana Health in your answer. [2]
(b) To what extent is it true that PCA should always be applied before training a model on high-dimensional data? Refer to Sabana Health in your answer. [4]
items.answer: (a) As dimensions increase, the distances between all points become similar, so the "nearest" neighbours are hardly nearer than others and data become sparse; many irrelevant dimensions also add noise to the distance. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (b) PCA is a useful tool but not automatic: it should be evaluated against model performance and the need for interpretability.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an outlier and noise.

items.answer: Wrapper methods train and evaluate a model for many candidate subsets of features, whereas filter methods compute a single statistic per feature.

items.answer: PCA is a linear method that preserves global variance and can transform new data; t-SNE is non-linear, preserves local neighbourhoods, and is used mainly for visualisation.

items.stem:
(a) Distinguish between label encoding and one-hot encoding. [2]
(b) A model uses the feature City with possible values Accra, Oslo, Seoul plus 6 numerical features. Using one-hot encoding with columns in alphabetical order (Accra, Oslo, Seoul), encode the rows Seoul, Accra, Seoul, Accra, Seoul, and state how many input features the model will have. Explain why label encoding (Lima = 1, Oslo = 2, …) could mislead a linear model. [4]
(c) "Domain experts should always be involved in feature engineering." To what extent do you agree with this statement? [8]
items.answer: (a) One-hot uses a binary column per category with no implied order; label encoding maps categories to integers, which implies an order and is suitable only for ordinal data. (b) Seoul → [0, 0, 1]; Accra → [1, 0, 0]; Seoul → [0, 0, 1]; Accra → [1, 0, 0]; Seoul → [0, 0, 1]. Total features = 6 + 3 = 9. Label encoding implies an order/size between cities that does not exist. (c) Expert involvement is highly valuable, especially for tabular data and in sensitive domains, but should be combined with data-driven selection.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] One-hot uses a binary column per category with no implied order; label encoding maps categories to integers, which implies an order and is suitable only for ordinal data. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions). (b) [4 marks] Encodings: Seoul → [0, 0, 1]; Accra → [1, 0, 0]; Seoul → [0, 0, 1]; Accra → [1, 0, 0]; Seoul → [0, 0, 1] (A2). Feature count 9 (A1). R1 artificial ordering. (c) [8 marks] Arguments for: experts know which derived quantities matter (e.g. BMI, debt ratio); helps avoid nonsensical or leaking features. (b) Zara writes: "Data cleaning is only needed for small datasets." Explain why this is inaccurate. [2]
(c) The following response times (ms) of a web server are being cleaned: 54, 37, 47, 2, 52, 37, 50, 100, 35. Using the 1.5 × IQR rule (quartiles found as medians of the lower and upper halves, excluding the median when n is odd), identify any outliers, and discuss whether they should be removed. [4]
items.answer: (a) Rescaling a feature to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 using (x − μ)/σ (b) Large datasets usually contain more errors, duplicates and inconsistencies; "garbage in, garbage out" applies at any scale. (c) Q1 = 36, Q3 = 53, IQR = 17; fences 10.5 and 78.5; outliers: 2, 100.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] 1 mark for the core idea: rescaling a feature to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 using (x − μ)/σ. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0. (b) [2 marks] Large datasets usually contain more errors, duplicates and inconsistencies; "garbage in, garbage out" applies at any scale. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation. (c) [4 marks] Q1 = 36, Q3 = 53, IQR = 17; fences 10.5 and 78.5; outliers: 2, 100. M1 sorted data/quartiles; A1 IQR and fences; A1 outliers. R1: remove only if errors (e.g. impossible values); genuine extreme values may carry information (e.g. real delays).

items.stem: A lender's dataset has Debt = 17 k$ and Income = 76 k$ for an applicant. Engineer a debt-to-income ratio and explain why it may predict default better than either raw feature.
items.answer: 17/76 = 0.224. It measures affordability relative to income: the same debt is riskier for a lower income.
items.markingKey: 0.224 (A1); R1 relative measure; R1 reduces dependence on scale.

items.stem: Each feature is divided into 4 intervals, so the feature space is split into cells. Compare the number of cells for 5 feature(s) and 10 features, and the number of training samples needed for about 5 samples per cell. Explain what this shows about the curse of dimensionality.
items.answer: 4^5 = 1024 cells vs 4^10 = 1048576 cells; for 5 samples per cell you need 5120 vs 5242880 samples. The data needed grows exponentially with dimensions, so data becomes sparse.
items.markingKey: 4^5 = 1024 cells vs 4^10 = 1048576 cells; for 5 samples per cell you need 5120 vs 5242880 samples. A1 each count; R1 exponential growth → sparsity, distances become less meaningful, more data or fewer dimensions needed.

items.stem:
A customer dataset contains these records (Name, City, Age):
Name | City | Age
Elena | Bogotá | 29
Arjun | Bogotá | 53
Lukas | Kuala Lumpur | 26
Arjun | Bogotá | 53
Jonas | Melbourne | 33
Ingrid | Dubai | 62
Lukas | Kuala Lumpur | 26
Ingrid | Dubai | 62
How many exact duplicate rows must be removed, and how many records remain? Explain why duplicates harm a model.
items.answer: 3 duplicates removed; 5 records remain. Duplicates over-weight some examples, bias the model and can leak between training and test sets.
items.markingKey: 3 duplicates (A1); 5 remain (A1); R1 bias/over-weighting/leakage.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that Domain experts should always be involved in feature engineering.
items.answer: Expert involvement is highly valuable, especially for tabular data and in sensitive domains, but should be combined with data-driven selection.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: experts know which derived quantities matter (e.g. BMI, debt ratio); helps avoid nonsensical or leaking features. Arguments against: deep learning can learn features automatically from raw data; experts may carry biases or overlook unexpected patterns; cost and availability of experts. Supported judgement: Expert involvement is highly valuable, especially for tabular data and in sensitive domains, but should be combined with data-driven selection.

items.stem:
Case study context: Harvest Link, an agricultural cooperative near Nairobi, records crop sales in a database, uses sensors and a model to predict yields, and gives farmers an app that queues orders and caches prices in a hash table.
(a) Explain why k-nearest neighbours performs poorly in very high-dimensional spaces. Refer to Harvest Link in your answer. [2]
(b) "PCA should always be applied before training a model on high-dimensional data." Discuss. Refer to Harvest Link in your answer. [4]
items.answer: (a) As dimensions increase, the distances between all points become similar, so the "nearest" neighbours are hardly nearer than others and data become sparse; many irrelevant dimensions also add noise to the distance. (b) PCA is a useful tool but not automatic: it should be evaluated against model performance and the need for interpretability.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] Award marks for: As dimensions increase, the distances between all points become similar, so the "nearest" neighbours are hardly nearer than others and data become sparse; many irrelevant dimensions also add noise to the distance. (one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.) (b) [4 marks] Arguments for: reduces dimensionality, training time and overfitting; removes correlated features; enables visualisation. Arguments against: components are hard to interpret; variance is not the same as predictive relevance – useful low-variance features can be discarded; not suitable for non-linear structure. Supported judgement: PCA is a useful tool but not automatic: it should be evaluated against model performance and the need for interpretability. Credit is given only for points applied to the stated organisation (not generic answers).

items.stem: To what extent is it true that Data cleaning is the most important stage of a machine-learning project?
items.answer: It is among the most important stages because no algorithm can compensate for poor data, but it must be balanced with sound modelling and evaluation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: model quality is limited by data quality; practitioners report most time is spent on preparation; errors and bias in data propagate into predictions. Arguments against: algorithm choice, features and evaluation also matter; over-cleaning can remove genuine signal; the importance depends on the data source. Supported judgement: It is among the most important stages because no algorithm can compensate for poor data, but it must be balanced with sound modelling and evaluation. Markbands (6 marks): top band: well-balanced discussion with accurate, specific technical detail applied to the context and a justified conclusion; middle band: some balance and correct terminology, conclusion only partly supported; bottom band: descriptive, largely one-sided, little technical detail or application.

items.stem:
Case study context: Aurora Energy, a utility in Toronto, collects smart-meter readings in a distributed database, detects faults with anomaly detection and models its devices as objects in a simulation.
(a) Explain the difference between label encoding and one-hot encoding. Refer to Aurora Energy in your answer. [2]
(b) "Domain experts should always be involved in feature engineering." To what extent do you agree with this statement? Refer to Aurora Energy in your answer. [4]
items.answer: (a) One-hot uses a binary column per category with no implied order; label encoding maps categories to integers, which implies an order and is suitable only for ordinal data. (b) Expert involvement is highly valuable, especially for tabular data and in sensitive domains, but should be combined with data-driven selection.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] One-hot uses a binary column per category with no implied order; label encoding maps categories to integers, which implies an order and is suitable only for ordinal data. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions). (b) [4 marks] Arguments for: experts know which derived quantities matter (e.g. BMI, debt ratio); helps avoid nonsensical or leaking features. Arguments against: deep learning can learn features automatically from raw data; experts may carry biases or overlook unexpected patterns; cost and availability of experts.
